newsitem.title: FINLAND: Summit boosts Russia's trade investment prospects.
newsitem.headline: Summit boosts Russia's trade investment prospects.

text.p: The United States agreed on Friday to back Russia's bid to join two world trade and financial bodies and offered to turn the next Group of Seven summit into the "Summit of the Eight".

Presidents Bill Clinton and Boris Yeltsin, at a meeting in Helsinki, also hammered out a plan to promote investment in Russia's struggling economy and agreed to work towards lifting trade barriers against Russian goods.

The initiatives addressed Moscow's demand to be admitted into the world economic club five years after it abandoned communism and the West's concern that it had not done enough to tackle corruption and press ahead with market reforms.
But while economists welcomed the pledges, they said that by themselves, they would change little.

Glossing over the vague nature of the agreements Yeltsin, who had accused the United States in the run-up to the summit of not doing enough to help Russian market reforms, told a news conference they reflected a totally new approach.
"Finally a breakthrough has been made," he said.

Clinton did the same, saying Moscow had shown its determination to reinvigorate market reform in a government reshuffle unveiled this week and had promised tax refoms and anti-corruption laws to improve the investment climate.
The two leaders said they would try to get Russia into the Paris Club of government creditors this year and into the World Trade Organisation (WTO) in 1998.
Moscow sees joining the Paris Club as a way to get back some of the money it is owed by Third World countries lent money by the Soviet Union during the communist era.
It wants to join the WTO to regulate its trading relations with other countries and reduce the chances of anti-dumping legislation putting up barriers to Russian exports.

Catherine Macdougall, Russia analyst at Kleinwort Benson in London, noted the decision on admitting Russia rested with many countries. "It wasn't up to the Americans to approve or disapprove of WTO or Paris Club membership," she said.
Other analysts saw drawbacks in the investment package.
Yeltsin pledged to put priority on a tax regime to stimulate legitimate business, including actions on the value-added tax, excise tax, and both corporate and individual income taxes."
For his part, Clinton pledged to step up financing for investment in Russia via various U.S. government agencies.

These included backing project finance, political risk insurance and investment funds through the Overseas Private Investment Corporation (OPIC) and expanding financing for equipment exports through the Export-Import Bank.
Deputy U.S. Treasury Secretary Lawrence Summers said later that funds already committed to OPIC and the bank would allow investment of up to $4 billion in Russia if conditions allowed.
"Private investment is driven not by decisions made at a summit, but by actions on the ground. There's still a way to go," said Charles Blitzer, economist at Donaldson, Lufkin and Jenrette in London.
On the trade front, progress seemed similarly distant.
Clinton and Yelstin said they would work to "establish the appropriate conditions to extend Most Favoured Nation status (MFN) to Russia on a permanent and unconditional basis."
MFN is the system under which the United States increases access to exports from certain trading partners.

Clinton said the Group of Seven leading industrial nations had agreed to give Russia a bigger role at its Denver summit meeting in June which, in a nod to Moscow's demands for full membership, would be called the Summit of the Eight.
But Summers later made clear that while Russia would join some economic discussions, this was not the G-8 that Russia wanted.
"It is fair to say there will be certain core financial issues that will continue to be discussed by the Seven. But other economic issues will be discussed by the Eight," he said.
